title: Binotto wants Slater in an F1 seat in the near future
excerpt:
Audi CEO Mattia Binotto has made no secret of his plans for Freddie Slater, stating in Azerbaijan that he wants the youngster “into an F1 seat” in the near future.

Slater signed with Audi as part of their Driver Development Programme earlier this year and has rewarded the team for their faith in him with a strong season in F3, where he finished runner up to Ugo Ugochukwu.

Slater has benefitted from working closely with Audi’s Racing Director Allan McNish, whose former role with the team was to run their junior academy, and the 18-year-old is set to graduate into the ranks of F2 next season, having signed with Invicta Racing.

Binotto was asked if Slater will take on more F1 duties in 2027, and the Italian was swift to reply.

"Or maybe even earlier," he said. "So, certainly Freddie is part of our driver development programme. High potential, he’s doing well. Just finished second in the championship.

“He was leading the championship before the last weekend in Madrid. Now finishing second. I think we discussed that with him. It can be as well a great lesson learned. Sometimes it’s not that, and that will be forgotten very soon.

“More important what he will deliver in the future. F1 duties yes, because that’s part of the development plan.”

Young drivers are given the opportunity to feature in free practice sessions in F1, with each team that does not have a full-time rookie in their ranks asked to give up four separate FP1 sessions across the season to run someone who might benefit from the experience.

Audi have been running Paul Aron in that role this season, sharing the Estonian with Alpine. But it sounds like Slater could step into the cockpit of the R26 sooner rather than later, especially given Audi have only fulfilled two of their four FP1 slots so far.

But as to where Slater goes in the future, that will depend on how he develops as a driver according to Binotto, not to mention how the current Audi incumbents, Gabriel Bortoleto and Nico Hulkenberg fare next season.

While Bortoleto is very much seen as the future of the team given his age, Hulkenberg will turn 40 midway through next season.

“F1 seat in the future, that will depend on how strong [Slater] will continue developing. But when you’ve got a driver in your academy, somehow the plans are for him, sooner or later, to be in your F1 seat,” Binotto explained.

“So again, happy with him, the way he has progressed. If you look at his F3 season since the start, where maybe he was abusing a bit too much on the tyres, he has become more balanced, managing better, getting experience and finishing very strong this season.”

title: Perez reflects on 'one of my best weekends'
excerpt:
Sergio Perez believes his performance in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix was "one of my best weekends" in Formula 1, despite failing to reach the points for Cadillac.

The streets of Baku have been a happy hunting ground for the Mexican, who took victories at the venue in 2021 and 2023 when driving for Red Bull, and Perez was hopeful of a strong result again last weekend.

Although Perez enjoyed his best practice outings of the season, the Cadillac driver ultimately fell short in Qualifying and could only manage P20, as well as receiving a three-place grid drop for impeding.

But in the race, Perez managed to stay in touch with the midfield runners on his way to P14 and his joint best result of the season.

"I think it's been one of my best weekends, best performance in Baku and I've had some good ones here," said Perez.

"I'm pretty pleased with that, I think I drove at a high level the whole weekend, especially in the race but we are simply a second, two seconds off the pace to compete with the others.

"We stayed the whole first stint with the Williams, with the Audi, helped by the overtake mode. But at the end, we just didn't have the straight-line speed, we are too draggy on the straights.

"Plenty of things we need to improve, but as we know, it's going to be a difficult end of the year."

Cadillac have still yet to score a point during their maiden season of F1, with Valtteri Bottas' P13 in China the team's best result so far.

While no major upgrades are expected before the end of the season, Perez hopes the team can improve in other areas in order to hit the ground running in 2027.

"I think we don't have anything coming to the car unfortunately but I think operationally and pushing the team to improve and get the maximum out of the weekends, I think we are heading in that direction," he said.

"We just have to keep pushing a lot harder as a team and things will come."

title: Who impressed our Power Rankings judges in Azerbaijan?
excerpt:
George Russell was the driver to beat throughout the Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend, as he charged to pole position and bagged an important win. But who else impressed our Power Rankings judges at the Baku City Circuit? Check out the latest scores and overall leaderboard below...

How it works

Our five-judge panel assess each driver after every Grand Prix and score them out of 10 according to their performance across the weekend – taking machinery out of the equation

Our experts’ scores are then averaged out to produce a race score – with those scores then tallied up across the season on our overall Power Rankings Leaderboard (at the bottom of the page)

Russell was back to his best on the streets of Baku – leading the way in Thursday practice, taking pole position by a whopping eight tenths of a second, and converting that into victory despite intense pressure from Red Bull’s Max Verstappen in the closing stages. Unsurprisingly, our judges could not fault his weekend performance.

Verstappen cut a hugely frustrated figure after Qualifying in Azerbaijan, with apparent power unit/battery issues leaving him back in eighth on the grid – a few hours after he had topped final practice. However, race day marked a big step in the right direction for driver and team, as the Dutchman cut his way through the field for a well-earned P2 finish, and very nearly the victory.

Isack Hadjar spent six weeks on the sidelines after injuring his wrist while training over the summer break, but you would not have known it based on the showing he delivered in Baku. Having steadily built up speed throughout practice, he earned a fine fourth position during Qualifying, and turned that into a “first proper podium on pure pace” in F1.

Pierre Gasly was understandably heartbroken when he arrived in the media pen after Saturday’s race. Pushing to turn an impressive P7 on the grid into another strong points haul, the Frenchman was taken out of the action by Alpine team mate Franco Colapinto, meaning they both went home empty-handed. “I don’t think I really have words, and I don’t need the words now,” Gasly sighed.

Esteban Ocon arrived in Azerbaijan stating that he is a “free agent” for 2027, with the Frenchman’s stint at Haas looking set to come to an end. Starting 14th after being impacted by yellow flags in Qualifying, Ocon did his talking on the track in the race by charging to eighth – ahead of team mate Ollie Bearman, and only just being beaten to the line by Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad.

Bearman had qualified a few spots ahead of Ocon in 11th – agonisingly close to Q3. He led Haas’ charge for most of the race, only to make contact with Kimi Antonelli at a Safety Car restart and open the door for his team mate to slip through. Still, P9 at the chequered flag marked a solid result, and ensured the squad got both cars in the points.

Lindblad experienced a rollercoaster weekend around the streets of the Azerbaijani capital. The F1 rookie put himself on the back foot with an FP2 crash for the second successive event, and subsequently placed 15th in Qualifying, after which he admitted to “trying to be too special”. Race day brought some more drama in the form of a collision with team mate Liam Lawson, but he nonetheless did well to cross the line in P7.

Charles Leclerc was left with mixed feelings after Qualifying in Baku. On the one hand, he was pleased to come away with P2, but on the other hand admitted to Russell’s pole advantage being much bigger than anticipated. In the race, he could do nothing to stop Piastri and the Red Bulls from slotting ahead, though reclaimed P4 when the McLaren man locked up into Turn 1 late on.

As mentioned above, Lawson had been the lead Racing Bulls driver in Azerbaijan on his return from Red Bull, only for Lindblad to tag him into a spin at the first Safety Car restart. “I love getting taken out by my team mate. That’s pretty sick,” he sarcastically commented on the radio afterwards. The New Zealander did what he could to make up lost ground, but ultimately had to settle for 12th.

Williams unleashed a raft of updates at the Baku City Circuit as they looked to breathe some life into their difficult 2026 season. It appeared to do the trick, with both drivers progressing to Q2 before Carlos Sainz pulled out a mighty lap and reached Q3. A post-session penalty for failing to adhere to yellow flags saw the Spaniard drop from ninth to 14th on the grid, but he made the most of the drama to come away with a morale-boosting point.

Sergio Perez was in a punchy mood after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, describing it as “one of my best weekends” in the sport after “driving at a high level” from FP1 to the chequered flag. He comfortably headed Cadillac’s efforts with the latest Ferrari power unit, managing to mix it with some of the midfield runners and come away with a respectable P14 – even if several retirements played their part.

Missing out

Just missing out on the Baku Power Rankings list are Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg, who came within a second of scoring a point, and the aforementioned Piastri and Antonelli – the former’s score impacted by that late lock-up, and the latter’s by his Q1 accident.

title: Sainz and Albon evaluate Williams’ Baku upgrades
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz recovered from a grid penalty in Baku to score for the first time in 10 rounds, but the Spaniard believes that Williams “need more” from their upgrades if they “want to fight for points regularly”.

The Grove-based outfit have struggled with an overweight car and additional performance issues for most of the 2026 season, leading to their decision to focus resources on a significant package introduced at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

It seemed to have an immediate impact as they enjoyed their first Q3 appearance of the year with Sainz, although he was later penalised with a five-place grid drop after failing to slow for yellow flags.

Aided by retirements for drivers further ahead, he improved from P14 to P10 to add a point to Williams’ tally, but was left with mixed feelings from the weekend as a whole.

“I think [it’s] what we deserved this weekend, to get a point for the team after the effort of the upgrade and a great Qualifying yesterday,” Sainz said. “Some good management there at the end for the last 10-15 laps, getting myself back into contention.

“I’m very disappointed after what happened yesterday, the way that was managed, the way that was handled. I was very depressed, let’s say, going into today. I managed to get a point for the team which was the target.

“[There’s] optimism in terms of I think the package is going to allow us to get back into positions where we can have some fun and fight with the others. The reality is that to get points, we’re still going to need each other’s help or some people’s help.

“I think the package is good to see, but after what I saw today, I think we’re going to need more if we want to fight for points regularly.”

For his team mate Alex Albon, the race in Baku was one to leave in the past – he locked up and crashed into the wall, triggering a Safety Car that ultimately led to restart chaos that eliminated multiple drivers.

Reflecting on the error, Albon explained: “Unusual crash, unusual place. I’ve not fully understood – maybe I braked a little later than the last lap, had a tailwind. We don’t like that corner as well, so we generally front-lock there. My fault, but it happens.”

He was nevertheless satisfied with the early performance of the upgrades, which included a new floor and adjustments to the rear of the car, but agreed with Sainz that further improvements should be made.

“We probably need a bit more aero in the car,” he said. “Actually, this car was not bad. This track suited us, our pace was actually quite good throughout the race. In the two medium speed corners of the track – Turn 1 and the last corner – we were slow, which is going to make the rest of the year difficult.”

title: 'Less pressure on me than there is him' – Russell on title
excerpt:
George Russell won his third Grand Prix of the season with victory in Baku, the Mercedes man standing on the top step of the rostrum for the first time since Austria.

In doing so, he cut his team mate’s lead in the Drivers’ Championship, Kimi Antonelli now 66 points ahead in the standings.

Antonelli arrived in Azerbaijan with an 81-point advantage over Russell following his back-to-back victories in Monza and Madrid. That translated to over three race wins, meaning the Italian could DNF at all three Grands Prix of this triple-header and still head to Austin in the lead.

Russell was in dominant form in Baku, topping two of the practice sessions before taking pole by the biggest margin of the season. His championship hopes were then aided by Antonelli crashing in Q1, and thus only qualifying 16th.

It was arguably the first big mistake from Antonelli since China, and while the 20-year-old recovered to finish fifth, Russell’s win saw him gain 15 points on his rival.

“There’s much less pressure on me than there is him," said Russell. "As I said [Friday], he’s had an incredibly flawless season. [Qualifying] was probably his first mistake of this whole season in a proper session... and he still came home in P5.”

“I didn’t really consider myself in this fight for a number of races, purely because my performance wasn’t strong enough. Now I feel like if the season were to have started today, or since the summer break, you know, I feel very much I would have been able to fight.

“Now I’ve got this big deficit. It can change quick. So, I’m not chasing that. I’m chasing to win every race, and what will be, will be.”

Antonelli vows to take lessons from ‘worst weekend of the season’

Russell has admitted already this season that he is not quite getting on as well with the new generation of cars as his team mate, despite a strong start to the year with pole and the win in Australia.

When he then took pole for the Sprint in Shanghai and won that dash, it looked like he was justifying his pre-season tag as favourite for the title. But after China, Russell didn't make the podium for four rounds, and was not helped by a run to the summer break that included a DNF in Spa and only seventh in Hungary.

Last season after Round 15, Oscar Piastri led Lando Norris by 34 points in the standings, with Max Verstappen a staggering 104 points behind the Australian. And yet come Abu Dhabi, Norris won the title, finishing 13 points ahead of his team mate and just two points clear of Verstappen.

That was a 47-point swing from Piastri to Norris, and a 115-point swing from Piastri to Verstappen. In such light, Russell’s 66-point deficit does not look quite so insurmountable, especially considering the Briton’s current form.

Whether the pressure will start to tell on Antonelli remains to be seen. He drove a sensible, considered race in Baku to recover to fifth, not taking any risks and not scything his way through the field with the same swagger he managed in Monza.

But if his team mate keeps performing like he did in Azerbaijan, Antonelli might find things are only going to get harder form here on out.

title: Norris apologises to Colapinto for Baku post-race comments
excerpt:
Lando Norris has apologised to Franco Colapinto for comments he made immediately after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, admitting “it was wrong of me” to do so.

Colapinto locked up and went too deep at Turn 1 during the first Safety Car restart at the Baku City Circuit, taking out both Alpine team mate Pierre Gasly and the McLaren of Norris.

The stewards subsequently gave Colapinto a 10-second time penalty, which was converted into a five-place grid drop for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, given that the Argentinian did not finish Saturday’s race.

Speaking in the media pen following his own retirement, Norris stated that there are “some drivers that shouldn’t be in F1”, while also suggesting Colapinto should be banned.

On Monday, with the dust settling on the situation, Norris took to social media to explain that he had directly apologised to Colapinto, and they “are still good friends”.

“Tough weekend overall in Baku and of course a disappointing and early end to the race,” read a statement posted by Norris on Instagram.

“After the race, I sent Franco a message apologising for the comments I made that I simply should not have said. I know better and emotions were running high but that is not an excuse, it was wrong of me.

“I’ve made mistakes of my own over the years and I know this is very much a part of racing and fighting on the limit.

“Me and Franco came to a good understanding, are still good friends and are both excited to get back racing this weekend.”

title: Vasseur offers Ferrari upgrade promise to frustrated Leclerc
excerpt:
Ferrari Team Principal Fred Vasseur has promised that the Maranello-based squad will bring developments to the SF-26 “soon” after Charles Leclerc cited a lack of recent development as a reason behind their poor form in Azerbaijan.

Baku specialist Leclerc qualified second, an outcome that even surprised the team given the straight-line speed deficit that has been apparent all season.

However, race day brought something of a reality check when he slipped down the order to P5 in the opening laps as he was unable to defend.

In the end, a mistake by Oscar Piastri allowed Leclerc to finish P4, having fallen off the lead battle at around a second a lap in the mini sprint that followed the last Safety Car interlude.

With Lewis Hamilton having to settle for P6, it was not a great outcome for a team that have won twice this year – especially at a track where Leclerc often shines.

It wasn’t just about a straight-line performance deficit, as Hamilton cited his struggles to get the tyres into the right temperature window as a major factor behind his disappointing weekend.

“Honestly, we were surprised to be on the first row, because it’s one is the most demanding on the engine, and we were not expecting to do so,” said Vasseur.

“But we knew even starting from the first row that the opening laps, or in case of restarting after a Safety Car and so on, it would be difficult, and it was. But overall, I think that we maximised what we can do in Baku with P4 and P6. For us, we can't be satisfied with P4 and P6, but in Baku I think it’s the maximum.”

Ferrari’s performance on the straights has been an issue all season, and the team have had to make compromises to compensate.

“The biggest limitation is that when you are in this situation and you want to defend, you go in a kind of negative spiral,” said Vasseur. “Perhaps to try to run a bit lower downforce than say optimum, because you need to defend, and you are losing lap time.

“We had a similar case in Monza. There the pace was decent. The quali position was decent, but we were losing one position per straight line in the opening laps.

“The next races are a bit less demanding than this one. Let’s try to be back. And there is also a kind of convergence on the chassis, you can improve much quicker than with the engine. There is a kind of convergence of performance on the chassis.”

Hinting at recent improvements by rivals, he added: “I think the advantage that we had on the chassis is smaller, or not there anymore.”

Regarding Leclerc’s call for much-needed upgrades, Vasseur insisted that the wait won’t be long.

“I won’t give you the date, but soon,” he said. “Now it’s like this that we are all bringing upgrades at different places. I think McLaren did something this weekend, and Merc it will probably be next weekend, with Malaysia and [Kuala Lumpur-based Title and Technical Partner] Petronas.

“We will do it as soon as possible. For sure, sometimes you do steps, but it’s not always paying off, because sometimes you have to fine tune. Now I think everybody is switching to the next year’s programme, because even if it’s into the continuity, we have some changes on the regulations, and we have to anticipate this.”

title: Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Every time F1 raced using a different country's name
excerpt:
This weekend we will have a grand prix held in a different country from the name it suggests - but what other instances of this have we seen during F1's history?

F1 arrives at Sepang this week for a race that will not go anywhere near the country in its name.

The Bahrain Grand Prix has been relocated to Malaysia, with the Sepang International Circuit hosting the Gulf Air-backed event after Bahrain International Circuit was ruled out following a postponement of the original April date and subsequent security concerns across the Middle East.

Bahrain is understood to be helping fund the move, while retaining its national airline's title sponsorship.

It is far from the first time a grand prix name and its venue have gone their separate ways.

The 1982 Swiss Grand Prix

Switzerland has not hosted a round of the world championship on home soil since 1954, after the country banned circuit motor racing in the wake of the 1955 Le Mans disaster.

That did not stop the calendar from carrying a Swiss Grand Prix in 1982, run instead at Dijon-Prenois in France.

Keke Rosberg won from eighth on the grid for Williams, with Alain Prost's Renault second and Niki Lauda completing the podium for McLaren.

The 1981-2006 San Marino Grand Prix

For 26 years, the San Marino Grand Prix was one of the fixtures of the European season, and yet the race never came close to the tiny republic whose name it carried.

FIA rules allowed each nation only one national grand prix, and Italy's was already spoken for by Monza. San Marino, in any case, had neither the terrain nor an FIA-standard circuit to host F1.

The solution was to borrow the neighbouring enclave's identity for a race staged at Imola, just across the Italian border, which became a fixture of the calendar until its final running in 2006.

The 1997-1998 Luxembourg Grand Prix

The same logic produced the Luxembourg Grand Prix, held in 1997 and 1998 not in Luxembourg but at the Nurburgring in Germany.

Hockenheim already held the contractual rights to the German Grand Prix, and regulations barred two races in the same country from sharing a national title, so organisers reached for Luxembourg instead, whose border sits roughly 80 kilometres from the Nürburgring.

Jacques Villeneuve won the 1997 edition for Williams ahead of Jean Alesi's Benetton, while Mika Hakkinen took victory in 1998 from Michael Schumacher's Ferrari.

The many locations of the European Grand Prix

The European Grand Prix name went further still, appearing across six circuits in three different countries: Brands Hatch and Donington Park in Britain, the Nürburgring in Germany, Jerez and the Valencia street circuit in Spain, and Baku in Azerbaijan.

The title was historically used as a way of squeezing a second race into a country's season without breaching the one-grand-prix-per-nation rule, and it also served as the promotional label for Baku's inaugural 2016 race before the event was renamed the Azerbaijan Grand Prix the following year.

title: Ferrari issue unusual statement amid rampant Fred Vasseur-Christian Horner rumours
excerpt:
Ferrari has declared that it has "full confidence" in team principal Fred Vasseur, amid growing speculation linking Christian Horner to the team.

In an interview with The Times last week, Horner declared that Ferrari was the "dream job" and that it was the only team he would be prepared to join on the grid as a mere employee, and not accept a role in the ownership structure - something he has made clear he wants following his exit from Red Bull in July 2025.

Vasseur addressed the reports after the Azerbaijan GP, declaring that he had "the best job in the world", but RacingNews365 understands from well-placed sources that discussions had taken place over how a potential Vasseur departure would look at the end of the current season.

Ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia this weekend, Ferrari took the extraordinary step of hastily arranging a news conference to address the speculation - where Vasseur received a full vote of confidence.

"In recent days, there has been increasing speculation surrounding Ferrari and particularly dedicated to its leadership," Ferrari's chief communications officer, Maria Conti said.

"Ferrari's position is clear, has not changed, and Ferrari has made its choices already, and we have confidence, full confidence, in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so.

"At this time and in this particular moment, it's really important that the team remains united and cohesive, and we are focused all the energy, on the work ahead, Ferrari has always attracted extraordinary interest, and it is only natural that many professionals aspire to be part of it.

"It is a reflection of the strength of what Ferrari really represents. So this is why we really want to avoid, and we do not intend to fuel speculation or comment on assumption coming from outside the company, and is not just related to the story in The Times of Mr. Horner, but in general there is a lot of speculation about that.

"So again, we have confidence in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so.

"And the position is clear, not just now. We have already confirmed in the past. Our focus now is on the work. We would like, of course, to be focused on the future, and this is always the Ferrari spirit and the spirit of our founder: humility and complete focus on the future.

"We are doing that today, on Tuesday, 29th September, because we would like to avoid that in the next weekend in Malaysia being occupied only with this kind of gossip and speculation, but we would like to be focused on the race, on the performance, on the team, on Fred, and of course the leadership is taking to bring ahead the Scuderia Ferrari HP."

When then asked why CEO John Elkann and CEO Bernadetto Vigna had not made any public statements backing their team principal, Conti added that Elkann and Vigna had confidence in Vasseur and that Ferrari had "made its choices", in favour of Vassuer.

title: F1 teams at the mercy of Pirelli gamble in Malaysia
excerpt:
This year’s Bahrain Grand Prix will be held in Malaysia, which poses a difficult problem for tyre supplier Pirelli as the sport returns to the venue after nine years.

F1 teams will be facing various unknowns this weekend in Malaysia as the sport returns to the Sepang International Circuit for the first time in nine years.

With many of the teams relying on historical data for their pre-weekend estimations, this is also the case for tyre supplier Pirelli.

Just 10 weeks separated the announcement of Sepang's return on July 26 and race day on October 4.

Normally, Pirelli bases its compound choice for a weekend on a range of data, ideally recent, covering tyre degradation and grip levels at the circuit in question.

But with limited time available, Pirelli opted to decide its tyre compounds based on the information it had from its last visit to Malaysia.

"Since 2011, I think we went all the years, so we have a good history," said Pirelli head of motorsport Dario Marrafuschi.

"2017 was the first year with wider tyres at that time compared to the previous one, and in terms of balance between tyre size and vehicle package, it was reasonably close to what we have today.

"To answer your question, I would base our decisions on 2017 results, and would go for a choice in line with what we did that year, not in 2016, 2015, or 2014."

Grand Prix

Bahrain GP

Big question mark for teams

Pirelli has confirmed that it will bring the C2 (hard), C3 (medium), and C4 (soft) to Sepang this weekend.

In certain cases, such as new or returning venues, Pirelli sends personnel to the location to map everything out in advance, and that forms the basis for the selection of the three compounds brought to the race.

But this was not possible on this occasion, as the Italian marque simply did not have the time to carry out the job.

"We will not have enough time to send some people there to make the measurements because we need to prepare the materials as soon as possible," Marrafuschi added.

"I don't think we can send anyone to look at the asphalt before."

Pirelli's decision makes it somewhat a shot in the dark, as it is relying on nine-year-old data for its assumptions.

This also makes it difficult for the teams to prepare for the weekend, since not only has the current generation of cars not yet raced there, but neither has the previous ground-effect generation.

Of course, they can test a few things on the simulator, but there are still major gaps in the available track data. This means the teams also can't use the simulator to verify whether the tyres are actually suitable for the track.

title: The 10 drivers who raced when F1 last visited Malaysia
excerpt:
F1 returns to the Sepang International Circuit this weekend, with the venue set to host the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

It will be the first time the sport has raced at Sepang since the 2017 Malaysian Grand Prix, the final round of a contract that had been in place since 1999.

That farewell weekend in October 2017 produced one of the most memorable races of the season. Max Verstappen took a dominant victory for Red Bull, Lewis Hamilton secured second to extend his championship lead ahead of Daniel Ricciardo, and Sebastian Vettel charged from last to fourth before a bizarre cooldown-lap collision with Lance Stroll.

Nine years on, the championship is radically different from when the cars last fired up in Malaysia. New regulations, new power units, new teams.

But remarkably, 10 drivers on the current grid were also on the grid at Sepang in 2017.

Charles Leclerc, too, was on track that weekend. The Monégasque driver, still a few months from his F1 debut, drove Marcus Ericsson's Sauber in FP1, setting the 16th-fastest time in the session and outpacing regular driver Pascal Wehrlein.

It was one of four Friday practice outings Leclerc completed with Sauber that year before securing a full-time race seat for 2018.

Pierre Gasly, meanwhile, made his F1 debut at that very race. The Frenchman had been drafted in by Toro Rosso to replace the struggling Daniil Kvyat, fresh from winning the 2016 GP2 Series title and racing in Super Formula in Japan. He qualified P15 and finished P14 on his maiden outing, the beginning of a career that now spans nearly a decade.

title: Mahindra makes Nyck de Vries and Edoardo Mortara decision as Formula E driver pairing confirmed
excerpt:
Mahindra has confirmed that Edoardo Mortara and Nyck de Vries will remain with the team for the 2026/27 Formula E season.

The campaign marks the start of a new era for the series, with Formula E introducing its fourth-generation car, the Gen4, billed as the fastest machine in the championship's history.

Mortara and de Vries have driven for Mahindra since 2023, and together have taken two victories, 10 further podium finishes and six pole positions across their time with the team.

Their form last season helped the team to a record-equalling result, with Mahindra matching its best-ever finish of third in the teams' championship and scoring a record 252 points, its highest single-season tally to date.

The pairing will now lead the team into the Gen4 era, giving Mahindra continuity alongside proven race-winning experience as it aims to push further towards the front of the grid.

For Mortara, it will be a 10th season in Formula E, and the Swiss-Italian will have raced across all four generations of the championship by the time Gen4 makes its debut. He has six victories and 18 podium finishes in the category, finished runner-up in Season 7, fought for the title deep into the Season 8 finale, and remained in mathematical contention entering the Season 12 finale.

De Vries, meanwhile, enters his seventh season in the championship having made his debut after winning the 2019 Formula 2 title.

The Dutchman won the Formula E drivers' championship in just his second season, and has 15 podium finishes and six career wins to his name, two of which came last season as part of Mahindra's record campaign.

With both drivers now starting their fourth season together at the team, the deal gives Mahindra a settled base heading into Formula E's next chapter.

Why Mahindra opted for continuity over fresh faces

Mahindra CEO and team principal Frederic Bertrand explained the thinking behind retaining the duo.

"I would like to thank Nyck and Edoardo for continuing this adventure with us as we begin its second chapter," said Bertrand. "Over the past three seasons, we have built trust, shared reference points and a strong way of working together. That continuity will be important as Formula E enters the Gen4 era.

"Gen4 will bring an even greater challenge, and Season 13 will demand a steep learning curve from the whole team. We have a strong foundation, but there is still a great deal to discover about the new car. Our priority will be to learn quickly, work through the details and improve step by step."

For Mortara, the veteran will turn 40 ahead of the third round of the new season in Mexico City, with Lucas di Grassi's retirement making him the oldest driver on the grid.

It is a title which will not bother him, with Mortara pleased to extend his stay with Mahindra into a new era.

"I'm really happy to continue with the team," expressed Mortara. "Our collaboration over the past three seasons has been very positive, with results steadily improving along the way.

"Together, we've lifted our performance at every level, and I'm proud of what we've built. Entering my tenth Formula E season, we know the year ahead will be a real challenge, especially on the technical side, with so much that is new. I'm curious and excited to take on that challenge with the team as we move to the new Gen4 cars."

The most recent season was comfortably de Vries' best since returning to the championship after his dire spell in Formula 1 with AlphaTauri.

He was consistently one of the quickest drivers, and had it not been for a few incidents, would have been a real title contender. Based on the expected driving-style similarities between the Gen4 and F2, de Vries could be a driver to absolutely watch.

"The past three years with Mahindra have been a very rewarding journey," began de Vries. "We've made a lot of progress together, and finishing third in the teams' championship last season was a great reward for all the hard work everyone across the team has put in. I'm very proud of what we've achieved together and the direction we've been moving in.

"I'm very happy to continue with Mahindra as we enter the Gen4 era. It represents a completely new challenge for everyone in Formula E, with a lot to learn and discover. I'm excited to take that on with the team and see where this next chapter takes us."

title: Isack Hadjar dismisses Red Bull restrictions: 'I'm not five years old'
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has hit back at the suggestion that Red Bull could restrict certain extracurricular activities after he injured his wrist while training during the F1 summer break.

Hadjar quipped that he is not "five years old" when it was queried as to whether the Milton Keynes-based team might look to limit what he gets up to outside of the paddock.

"No," the two-time podium finisher replied to media, including RacingNews365, when asked if Red Bull had restricted certain activities, including boxing, after his injury.

Hadjar: 'There are no restrictions'

Hadjar did concede that he will need to be more considered when boxing in the future, but was keen to stress he can make his own decisions.

"Next time I'll just be more careful," he added. "You know, maybe strap myself, and that's it. It happens.

"There are no restrictions. I’m not five years old, so I just need to think twice before, you know…"

title: Sepang chaos revisited: five crazy Malaysian Grands Prix
excerpt:
A look back at five of the best in Malaysia from its fabulous era in F1.

Sepang hosted 18 editions of the Malaysian Grand Prix between 1999 and 2017, and few venues on the calendar built a reputation quite like it.

Hermann Tilke's first purpose-built circuit combined sweeping high-speed corners with a brutal tropical climate, and that combination produced some of the most chaotic afternoons in F1.

Monsoon downpours arrived with little warning, tyre degradation was merciless in the heat, and title fights repeatedly found their way to Sepang late in the season. The result was a run of races that swung championships and ended afternoons in a matter of laps.

Ahead of F1's return to Malaysia this weekend, with the Bahrain GP taking place in the country, picking the best five from 18 years is no small task, but these races stand out for the drama, the strategic gambles and the consequences that rippled well beyond the finish line.

Michael Schumacher comeback and a title thrown into chaos - 1999

The inaugural race at Sepang carried enormous stakes, arriving as the penultimate round of a title fight between Mika Häkkinen and Eddie Irvine.

Schumacher, returning from a broken leg, drove in support of Ferrari team-mate Irvine, helping the Ulsterman to victory ahead of Häkkinen. But the drama did not end at the flag.

Scrutineers subsequently disqualified both Ferraris over bargeboard dimensions, briefly handing the drivers' and constructors' championships to Häkkinen and McLaren, before the FIA Court of Appeal overturned the decision days later and restored Irvine's win.

Although Häkkinen went on to take the title in the final race in Japan, few results in the sport's history have been thrown into such doubt and then reinstated so dramatically.

Ferrari's monsoon masterclass - 2001

Michael Schumacher's win in only the second round of 2001 remains one of the most bizarre results of his career.

An early engine failure from another car left oil on the track, and when the rain arrived on lap three, both Ferraris of Schumacher and Rubens Barrichello slid into the gravel together.

Recovery looked improbable, but Ferrari's call to fit intermediate tyres during an extended safety-car pit stop, while rivals gambled on full wets, proved inspired.

As the track dried, both cars lapped seconds faster than the field. Schumacher took victory from Barrichello, with David Coulthard a distant third, in a result built entirely on a single strategic call.

© xpb.cc

Jenson Button's soggy confirmation - 2009

Jenson Button's Brawn had dominated the opening round in Australia, and Malaysia offered an early test of whether it was a genuine title package. The answer arrived through a downpour.

Torrential rain and fading daylight forced officials to red-flag the race on lap 33, with the final classification reverting to the order at the end of lap 31.

Button, who started from pole, was declared the winner, with Nick Heidfeld and Timo Glock completing the podium.

Because barely half the scheduled distance had been completed, only half points were awarded, for only the fifth time in F1 history, a quirk that later mattered in a tightly fought championship battle.

© XPBimages

Fernando Alonso conquers the storm - 2012

Fernando Alonso's Ferrari lacked the outright pace to challenge McLaren that weekend, as Lewis Hamilton and Jenson Button locked out the front row, but another Sepang storm changed the equation entirely.

A lengthy red-flag suspension turned the race into a tyre-crossover gamble, and Alonso's wet-weather execution proved decisive.

Sergio Pérez, on a remarkable run for Sauber, closed in late on the prime tyre and looked capable of snatching the lead, only for a wide moment at Turn 9 to end his challenge.

Alonso held on to win from Pérez and Hamilton, a result built on patience and tyre management rather than raw speed.

© XPBimages

Nico Rosberg takes title control after Lewis Hamilton engine blows - 2016

Few single mechanical failures have altered a championship as sharply as Lewis Hamilton's did in 2016.

Rosberg held an eight-point lead over his Mercedes team-mate going into what was the 16th round of the 21 that year.

Although Hamilton and Rosberg locked out the front row, the title picture looked set to change dramatically when Rosberg collided with Ferrari's Sebastian Vettel into Turn 1, dropping the former to the back of the pack.

Hamilton then looked set fare for victory until, on lap 41 of the 56, he suffered an engine failure after a sudden loss of oil pressure, ending his race in a plume of smoke.

Behind him, Rosberg recovered from his collision with Vettel to claim third, a damage-limitation drive that proved pivotal in the destination of that year's title.

Daniel Ricciardo took the win ahead of Max Verstappen for Red Bull's first one-two for three years, but the story of the day belonged to the gap Hamilton's retirement opened in the standings, one Rosberg never surrendered.

title: Red Bull reveal 'another edge' but handicapped by 'narrow window'
excerpt:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has claimed the team's upgrade package introduced at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix has given the outfit "another edge" over its F1 rivals, closing a gap that had been narrowing steadily since the start of the season.

The Milton Keynes-based team scored its first double-podium finish for two and a half years on Saturday, with Max Verstappen crossing the line 0.196 seconds behind race winner George Russell, and team-mate Isack Hadjar third.

However, it is still to end its victory drought this season, and is in danger of being without a win during a campaign for the first time since 2015.

Speaking about the team's development trajectory, Mekies pointed to the long stretch between the season-opening race in Australia and the Baku weekend, during which no major package had arrived, yet the gap to the front had still shrunk.

"As we have seen this year, the pecking order has been alternating based on the timing of the upgrades," said Mekies, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365.

"What is important, however, is that in the fairly long time frame between Australia and now, where we didn't have a big package coming, we have nonetheless managed to close that gap.

"If you look at Madrid [Spanish GP], we were a tenth and a half from pole, and I think we were two tenths from pole in Monza [three tenths to Alpine's Pierre Gasly].

"So we have managed to close that gap, with everyone in the team, on the chassis side, PU side, extracting from the actual car specifications.

"Then yes, the upgrade [in Baku] has given us another edge and eaten up that last tenth. We need to see how it will go on other tracks. How we then react to the other competitors, this I cannot say."

Red Bull's narrow window problem

But Mekies also acknowledged that Red Bull's power unit, while strong on outright potential, remains difficult to exploit consistently across a full lap and a full race distance.

The 2026 power units run without an MGU-H, leaving the 350kW MGU-K as the sole means of electrical harvesting, a change that has made energy management far more sensitive to circuit layout and deployment strategy across the grid.

Discussing the scale of the challenge his engineers have faced at Milton Keynes and trackside, Mekies said: "We have said a few times that we have a fantastic PU.

"But we have a fairly narrow band to use it at best, and it takes a lot of energy from everyone back in Milton Keynes, and at the racetrack, to try to keep us in the narrow window of performance. That's what we do every day.

"Every track comes with this chance of how you do that, and you hear it with our great communication with our drivers.

"Getting the right energy management, the right deployment, and the right power is certainly something that keeps us busy."

title: Will Christian Horner be next boss on Ferrari 'ejectable seat'?
excerpt:
They were understandable comments from Christian Horner, just published at the wrong time.

Over an Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend when the future of current Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur became a talking point in the paddock, a wide-ranging interview in The Times with Horner was aired.

Despite the nature of the article, which covered all aspects of Horner's life and career to promote the publication of his upcoming book, 'Drive', the headline said it all: Christian Horner: ‘Would I consider Ferrari? It’s the dream job’.

After 20 years with Red Bull, and despite the ignominious period he endured in 2024 before finally being sacked in July of last year, apparently for performance-related reasons, although Horner was told the team was "more Christian Horner Racing than Red Bull Racing", why wouldn't he consider Ferrari if "the dream job" became available? Who wouldn't?

Unfortunately, for Horner, the publication of The Times article, which RacingNews365 can confirm was written in early September, just so happened to go to press and coincide with the rumours surrounding Vasseur in Baku.

Additionally, the interview was arranged by the book's publisher, and not Horner himself, who was then naturally at the mercy of when it would be printed and, in tandem, go online.

[Article continues below]

© XPBimages

The barren Ferrari years

In The Times interview, Horner made clear that Ferrari was the one team he would renege on his previous remarks that for him to return to F1, it would have to be in an ownership role.

"I've been a hired hand," he said. "I did 21 years sitting on the pit wall. I don't need to go back to that. At this stage in my life, there's only one team for which I would accept non-participation in ownership."

As to the team, in particular, he added: "Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It's the dream. And arguably it's the sleeping giant of Formula 1."

That last bit is true.

This is Vasseur's fourth season in charge after taking over the helm at the start of 2023. The laconic Frenchman has imposed his way of working on Ferrari - direct, no holds barred, and unafraid to make changes and ruffle feathers.

It was an approach that came within a few points of landing Ferrari an elusive championship in 2024, only to agonisingly finish 14 points shy of McLaren at the end of a record-equalling 24-race season.

The insufferable wait to end the silverware drought, stretching back almost two decades to Kimi Raikkonen's drivers' triumph in 2007 and the last team crown a year later, goes on for the tifosi, and all connected with the Maranello marque.

The fact that change at the top is again being mooted comes on the back of a disappointing campaign this year in which Ferrari was fully expected to take the new regulations by the scruff of the neck and strangle out of them at least one trophy.

The SF-26, however, whilst strong in the chassis department, has been found wanting with its power unit. Even after two ADUO updates now, designed to help it draw level with the strongest ICE on the grid, belonging to PU newcomers Red Bull-Ford, it is still lacking.

And so the speculation over Vasseur's future has started to gather momentum, despite the fact he has a contract through to the end of next season at least. Allied to additional rumours of a health issue, there is growing suspicion he would be allowed to leave gracefully at the end of the year.

[Article continues below]

© XPBimages

Would Horner prove divisive?

If that proves to be the case, Ferrari chairman John Elkann and CEO Benedetto Vigna will already have sounded out potential replacements.

Antonello Coletta, currently in charge of Maranello's World Endurance Championship programme, is undoubtedly one, although it is understood he has previously rebuffed any advances.

Jérôme d'Ambrosio, currently Ferrari's deputy team principal, is another. However, whilst he would present a smooth transition, he is a Vasseur hire and this, along with his lack of experience at such a senior level, would likely count against him.

And then there is Horner, who met with Elkann at his Oxfordshire home four years ago to discuss the possibility of replacing Mattia Binotto, only to turn the opportunity down, leading to Vasseur's eventual appointment.

The reason Horner rejected it then, and it will undoubtedly come into the equation again, is one of autonomy. At that stage, in 2022, when Red Bull was in its second ascendancy, and the team and Max Verstappen were masters of all they surveyed, Horner was in a similar position as team principal and CEO.

Dietrich Mateschitz was a staunch Horner ally. Although the Briton lacked power via any shareholding, he wielded it through the corridors at Milton Keynes, with little interference from Red Bull's billionaire benefactor.

Horner and Red Bull's world changed significantly when Mateschitz passed away in October that year. So began an internal power struggle that ultimately culminated in the 52-year-old's exit nearly 15 months ago.

You would assume that should Horner and Elkann meet again - and they just so happened to be in Naples at the same time this week for the Louis Vuitton Cup, the preliminary regatta to the America's Cup - the Briton would seek assurances regarding just how much power inside Maranello he would have, and how much interference there would be from Elkann and Vigna.

Horner would want to stamp his own authority on proceedings, and hire people he felt he could trust to do the job required to turn Ferrari into serial winners again. How many noses would that put out of joint of those currently working at Ferrari?

Horner would not be afraid, that's for sure, but for Elkann and Vigna, they know they would be hiring a figure that even by his own admission is "a Marmite character". There would be people with him, and those against. Could the potential divisions be worth the drama if Ferrari finally became champions again?

[Article continues below]

© XPBimages

For now, Vasseur is aware of the spotlight he is under, one that will only grow in intensity as the season reaches its climax. He was under no illusion when asked about the situation following the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

He knows the situation 'is not in his hands', but he will fight on. "For sure," he said. "Motorsport is my life, my business. I'm trying to do my best. I'm there to do my job. I have the best job in the world, but it is like it is. We still have seven races to go, and I will push until the last corner."

It becomes a question of whether Elkann and Vigna feel the time is right for another change, and with Horner a free agent, whether he is the right man to lead a team starved of the success Red Bull enjoyed, under the Briton's leadership, over the 18 years since Ferrari last won anything of repute.

As 1997 F1 champion Jacques Villeneuve noted when asked about the possibility of Horner joining Ferrari, he is "someone you have to take seriously and under consideration because he amazingly built up Red Bull, the winning Red Bull".

That will be uppermost in the minds of Elkann and Vigna: that Horner is someone who knows what it takes to mastermind success.

But would Horner, despite his "dream" proclamation about joining Ferrari, be so willing to join a team unafraid to quickly jettison its top people when further years roll by without silverware?

As Villeneuve further noted: "We've seen so many changes, like two, three years, [then the] next one, because the results don't come, or for whichever reason.

"So you're always on an ejectable seat, and you really have to be careful."

Right now, Horner's comments to The Times, despite their unfortunate timing, have stirred a pot that constantly bubbles over at Ferrari.

title: Max Verstappen makes 'one second' declaration after George Russell defeat
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has conceded he likely would not have won the Azerbaijan Grand Prix even if he had started higher up in the order.

A challenging qualifying session for the Dutchman saw him line up for the start of the race in eighth position.

As he made his way through the field in the opening stint, he found himself behind George Russell after a safety car intervention shortly after the halfway stage.

Verstappen pushed to get in front of the Mercedes driver, but fell short at the line by just under two-tenths of a second, missing out on his first victory of the season.

While Verstappen possessed impressive speed during the race, he does not think it would have automatically translated to a position on the top step of the podium.

"Even if I had started second, I think [with] the pace of George, it would have been very hard to pass," Verstappen told media including RacingNews365.

"So maybe I could have followed him a bit better, of course, than in that first stint.

"Then you box, you're second, behind, and then probably we would have done the same race, just pushing each other along.

"It would have made my first stint a bit easier instead of overtaking all the cars that I had to.

"For sure the soft tyre was much better than the medium because the first few laps in the first stint were very strong.

"The tyres were just not working, and it was quite a bit of just surviving in the first stint, trying to go as long as possible."

[Article continues below]

Verstappen found final Baku stint 'very enjoyable'

Verstappen's headache of deciding when to switch over to the soft tyre was eased when a safety car was called following a crash involving Alex Albon.

As Verstappen pushed to try and get ahead of Russell, the Mercedes driver was able to match his pace as he held on for victory.

"And then the safety car actually came at the right time to swap to the soft tyres," Verstappen said.

"And then I have to say that those last laps were very enjoyable because there was barely any deg, really.

"We were just pushing to the end, and the gap was always, like, one second, 1.1, so that was nice.

"It looked close on the line, but I think that was more because I think George suffered from a little bit of boost lag in 15 with the yellow flag.

"So if you look at the last stint, it was always one second, so that's probably also where we would have finished."

title: Citroen name new Formula E team principal after Cyril Blais tragedy
excerpt:
Citroën Racing has confirmed Beth Paretta as its new team principal for the 2026/27 Formula E season, with Fred Espinos joining as deputy team principal as the squad reveals its first Gen4 livery.

Paretta steps up after serving as managing director throughout the team's debut campaign last season.

Espinos arrives from Lola Yamaha ABT, where he was deputy team principal, having previously worked as sporting manager at ABT Sportsline.

The appointments come after the tragic death of Cyril Blais, who held the team principal role before his passing was mourned across the Formula E paddock.

The championship paid tribute to him during the Tokyo double-header last July, where Nick Cassidy claimed back-to-back podiums for the team in his memory.

Citroen stick to iconic colours with full focus on Gen4 era

Citroën has stuck with the red, white and blue identity that proved popular with fans last season, now reworked for the more dynamic Gen4 machinery.

The reveal follows the team's confirmation earlier this month that it is reuniting with TotalEnergies for the GEN4 era, extending a partnership between the two French companies that dates back to 1968.

Cassidy and Jean-Eric Vergne remain in place as Citroën's full-time drivers for the upcoming campaign. Between them, the pair have 23 wins in Formula E, making them one of the most experienced line-ups on the grid.

Cassidy delivered the team's maiden win in just its second race, at the 2026 Mexico City E-Prix, with both drivers taking podiums across the calendar.

However, it is now all eyes on Gen4, with Paretta recognising it as a significant step up for the championship.

"GEN4 is much more than an evolution of the previous car: it is faster, more powerful and technologically more advanced, and it will change the way we approach race weekends," she said.

"For Citroën Racing, success will be about making the most of that opportunity from the very beginning. title: Liam Lawson handed staggering verdict over Racing Bulls future
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has been given an overwhelming vote of confidence going into the remainder of the F1 campaign.

Lawson has enjoyed a strong season so far with Racing Bulls, which has also included a three-race cameo with Red Bull after Isack Hadjar broke a wrist in training during the summer break.

The New Zealander has scored points in 10 of the 15 rounds, including highs of sixth in the Monaco, British and Spanish Grands Prix.

Racing Bulls, though, has yet to confirm its driver line-up for next season, in particular with Red Bull junior and F2 title challenger Nikola Tsolov pushing for a place on the F1 grid.

In a RacingNews365 poll, we asked whether Lawson had done enough to retain his seat.

[Article continues below]

Lawson did 'a very good job'

In one of the most comprehensive results we have seen, just under 95 per cent agreed that he deserved another year.

Just 2.5 per cent of voters felt another junior driver should be given a chance, while the remaining 2.5 per cent said the team should wait until the end of the season before making a call.

From the perspective of Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies and Racing Bulls counterpart Alan Permane, it is clear they feel Lawson has performed well this year, strongly pointing to the fact he will be handed a fresh deal for 2027.

"He's done a very good job," said Mekies recently on Lawson's short return to Red Bull. "I think we all know how difficult it is to jump to a different team, to a different car, and I think that he has done that to the best of what could have been our expectations.

"So, I think he did a very good job, again very different pictures compared to the first two races of 2025 when he was in the team, so we are thankful and happy with that."

Permane also pointed to Lawson's chemistry with team-mate Arvid Lindblad after he returned from his Red Bull cover duty.

"Much as we love Yuki [Tsunoda], and the whole team does, he's a very popular figure, it's good to have Liam back in his car, in the team, working very, very well with Arvid," said Permane. "Those two lift each other up through the weekend."

title: Engine guru confirms Max Verstappen was right: 'I already had this view'
excerpt:
The debate over the new engine generation shows no signs of abating anytime soon. While teams and the FIA are still fine-tuning the energy distribution, engine guru Mario Illien speaks out clearly in an interview with RacingNews365. His conclusion aligns almost perfectly with what Max Verstappen has been saying for months.

Max Verstappen made clear from the outset that he is not a fan of the current F1 power unit. Far from it.

Verstappen has at least garnered support for his critical point of view from renowned engine guru Mario Illien, the co-founder of Ilmor and the engineer behind years of Mercedes power units in F1.

Illien agrees with the four-time F1 champion that the balance between the combustion and electric in today's Formula 1 cars is wrong.

The Swiss engine designer, who has won numerous titles throughout his career, made his views clear in an exclusive interview with RacingNews365.

"I think there's just too much electric power in them," said Illien.

"I think the hybrid concept is fine, but not in this proportion. Racing with so much electric power shouldn't be a handicap. Moreover, it's very complex and very expensive, and it doesn't make the fans any more enthusiastic.

"It's not exciting on TV either when you see cars having to give up after just two-thirds of the straight. The driver's role becomes less important, and now software, and how you use it, is becoming more important than the racing itself."

[Article continues below]

Illien knows he and Verstappen are right

Verstappen has been one of the most outspoken critics of the current power unit era. During pre-season testing in Bahrain earlier this year, the Red Bull driver delivered a scathing verdict on the regulations, comparing the heavy energy management demands to racing in Formula E.

"As a driver, the feeling is not very Formula 1-like," Verstappen said at the time. "It feels a bit more like Formula E on steroids.

"As a pure driver, I enjoy driving flat out, and at the moment, you cannot drive like that. A lot is going on, a lot of what you do as a driver, in terms of inputs, which have a massive effect on the energy, and for me, that's just not Formula 1, and maybe it would be better to drive in Formula E, right, because that's all about energy efficiency and management."

When RacingNews365 pointed out that Illien's comments echo those remarks from Verstappen, the Swiss expert did not hesitate to agree.

"Yes," said Illien. "I already had this view before it all started. It was clear to me early on that this is how it would turn out."

[Article continues below]

The solution for F1?

The FIA is working on shifting the ratio between the internal combustion engine and electric power from the current 52/48 split to 58/42 next season, and 60/40 in 2028. Illien does not see that as a bad move, but stopped short of calling it a fix.

Asked whether that shift would be enough, he replied: "It will improve things a bit, that's for sure. But it won't solve the problem."

As for what the actual solution should be, Illien had no doubts. He said: "I think the ratio we had until last year was a good one; it worked.

"And no one really criticised it back then, because it was a sensible approach. I think it's good and useful to recover kinetic energy, that's also good for regular cars. But that kind of racing, I just miss it."

title: F1 driver ejected from car at 280 km/h in horrific crash - Throwback
excerpt:
F1 driver ejected from car at 280 km/h in horrific crash - Throwback

One of the most horrific non-fatal crashes in F1 history took place exactly 36 years ago today.

Thirty-six years ago today, on 28 September 1990, the life of Martin Donnelly changed forever.

The Northern Irish Team Lotus driver was regarded at the time as one of the biggest talents on the grid, backed by an impressive record in the junior categories.

Donnelly had built his reputation with victory in the prestigious Macau Grand Prix in 1987 and strong results in Formula 3000.

When he was handed a surprise call-up to replace an injured driver at Arrows during the 1989 French Grand Prix, he qualified comfortably ahead of his experienced team-mate Eddie Cheever.

The talent was obvious, and Donnelly had already signed a new multi-year deal for the following season.

Everything pointed towards a bright future in the top flight. Until one fateful Friday in Jerez.

On the brink of death

During qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix, the front suspension on Donnelly's Lotus-Lamborghini 102 failed.

A bell-crank came loose and gave way through a fast corner, and Donnelly lost all control of the steering. The floor of the car scraped along the asphalt before it speared into the barrier at around 280 kilometres per hour.

The impact was so violent that the carbon-fibre chassis snapped clean in two, tearing open the monocoque.

Donnelly was thrown from the wreck, still strapped to his seat, and landed separately on the track. Marshals did not need to cut him free from the car, because there was simply no wreck left to free him from.

FIA doctor Sid Watkins was among the first on the scene and immediately cleared the unconscious Donnelly's blocked airways to prevent him from choking. He suffered severe brain and lung injuries, along with multiple serious fractures to both legs and his collarbone.

He was placed in an induced coma in hospital due to organ failure and underwent several complex operations on his legs. At one stage, doctors even feared amputation.

Inspiration for an F1 movie

His recovery took years, with lengthy rehabilitation and lasting damage to his legs. Nerve damage left him physically unable to withstand the heavy pedal loads of a Formula 1 car, ruling out any return to the top flight.

Donnelly stayed involved in the sport regardless, working as a driver coach, running a junior team and serving as an FIA race steward.

He made occasional returns behind the wheel too, including in Lotus brand cup racing and, as late as 2015, once more in the British Touring Car Championship.

The crash itself led directly to stricter crash tests and tougher structural requirements for F1 monocoques, a legacy that still shapes every car on the grid today.

The accident did not stay confined to the history books either. It formed the direct blueprint for the backstory of lead character Sonny Hayes in the feature film F1.

The crash is visually recreated in the film, complete with a replica yellow Lotus 102 and overalls carrying Donnelly's sponsor logos from the time.

Producer Lewis Hamilton and the filmmakers contacted Donnelly beforehand to secure his approval and involve him in the scene.

title: Red Bull 'hierarchy' noted behind Baku team order debate
excerpt:
Red Bull was placed in a difficult position during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, but opted not to implement team orders.

Racing driver Alex Brundle has highlighted the "hierarchy" that exists at Red Bull as a key reason why its drivers did not swap positions during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

In the early stages of the race, Isack Hadjar was running behind his team-mate Max Verstappen but appeared to have more pace on the soft compound compared to Verstappen's medium.

The subject of team orders was floated at the time, but ultimately Red Bull opted not to switch their drivers around.

Brundle, however, did not see it as an unreasonable request.

"It's an interesting interplay between the two of them," Brundle told the F1 Nation podcast.

"The medium tyre worked so much worse on the Red Bull than the soft tyre did.

"I don't think it made a huge amount of difference to their eventual finishing positions when you look how far Isack was behind at the end of the race.

"But honestly, there was definitely a period where on the pit wall, I would have switched them back."

[Article continues below]

'Reasonable' to ask Verstappen to pull over

Verstappen went on to finish the race in second place, crossing the line just under two-tenths of a second down on winner George Russell.

The Dutchman has raced for Red Bull since early 2016 and has since established himself as one of the most successful drivers in the sport's history.

Over the last handful of years, he has faced no challenge from his team-mates and has consolidated his position as the team leader.

Brundle suggested that Red Bull did not wish to disrupt that stance by opting not to order a swap around of their drivers.

"Giving Isack a chance to overtake the McLaren was a reasonable thing to do, but it's still the Red Bull second seat.

"There's a hierarchy in that team, and they decided not to break it."
